entry: Natural satellites of the planet [[Uranus]]. Uranus has 29 known moons, 27 of which are named after characters in plays by [[William Shakespeare]] and in the poem *The Rape of the Lock* by [[Alexander Pope]]. The moons form three groups: fourteen inner moons, five major moons and ten irregular moons. The inner and major moons orbit prograde and are classed as regular moons, while the irregular moons have distant, highly inclined and mostly retrograde orbits. [[William Herschel]] discovered Titania and Oberon in 1787, William Lassell found Ariel and Umbriel in 1851, and Gerard Kuiper found Miranda in 1948. Most of the remaining moons were found after 1985, during the [[Voyager 2]] flyby or with advanced telescopes.

Observation on the growth of [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuits]]. Gordon Moore, co-founder of Fairchild Semiconductor and [[Intel]], noted in 1965 that the number of components per integrated circuit had been doubling every year. In 1975 he revised the forecast to doubling every two years, a compound annual growth rate of 41%. Despite the name, the law describes an empirical relationship rather than a scientific law. It has guided semiconductor planning and research targets, and is linked to falling prices of microprocessors and growing memory capacity. Since about 2010 industry advancement has slowed slightly below the predicted pace. In September 2022, Nvidia's then-CEO [[Jensen Huang]] considered the law dead, while Intel's then-CEO Pat Gelsinger took the opposite view.

Upland habitat of low-growing vegetation on acidic soils. Moorland, or moor, is closely related to heath, but moor refers to highland and high-rainfall areas, while heath refers to lowland zones more likely shaped by human activity. Moorlands are found mainly in tropical Africa, northern and western Europe, and South America. They are related to [[Tundra|tundra]], and the boundary between the two shifts with climatic change. In the [[British Isles]], heathland and moorland are the most extensive areas of semi-natural vegetation, and moors in eastern Britain are distinguished by a covering of peat. Biodiversity in the extensive moorlands of the tropics can be extremely high.

Historical exonym for mainly Muslim populations of North Africa, the [[Maghreb]], and the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. The name was applied in the [[Middle Ages]] and early modern period to Arabs, Berbers, Muslim Europeans and black peoples, so the Moors were not a single self-defined group. The term has racial connotations and has fallen out of scholarly use since the mid-20th century. The Romans called the Berber tribes of Mauretania *Mauri*, which became Moors in English. The historian [[Tacitus]] recorded the Moors revolting against the Roman Empire in 24 AD. Portuguese colonizers introduced the names Ceylon Moors and Indian Moors in Sri Lanka, and in the Philippines the Muslim community now calls itself the Moro people.

Largest extant species of [[Deer]], native to the boreal and temperate forests of the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. Called elk in Europe, the moose (*Alces alces*) is the tallest and the second-largest land animal in [[North America]], after the [[American bison]] in body mass. Adult males have broad, palmate antlers. Moose are solitary, feeding on twigs, bark and aquatic plants, with branches making up much of their winter diet. Predators include wolves, bears, humans, [[Wolverine|wolverines]] and, rarely, orcas. Males fight for females in autumn. [[Hunting]] and habitat loss reduced the species' range, and moose have been reintroduced to some former habitats, with the greatest populations now in Canada.

Family of flowering plants, commonly known as the mulberry or [[Fig|fig]] family. The family comprises about 48 genera and over 1,100 species, mostly in tropical and subtropical regions. Its members share latex-producing glands and milky sap, and the family includes the common fig, [[Breadfruit]], [[Jackfruit]] and mulberry. Their flowers are often pseudanthia, reduced inflorescences. Dioecy appears to be the primitive state in the family, and monoecy has evolved independently at least four times. The fossil record goes back to the late [[Cretaceous]]. Moraceae is placed in the order Rosales, and Cecropia, once placed in the family, is now in Urticaceae.

Accumulation of unconsolidated debris carried and deposited by a [[Glacier|glacier]] or [[Ice sheet|ice sheet]]. Moraines consist of glacial till, unsorted debris ranging from fine glacial flour and clay to sand, gravel and large boulders. Lateral moraines form along the sides of the ice, terminal moraines mark a glacier's maximum advance, ground moraines are till-covered sheets on irregular ground, and medial moraines form where two glaciers meet. Lateral moraines can rise up to 140 meters above the valley floor. Moraines form passively by dumping of supraglacial sediment or actively by glaciotectonic pushing. Reworking of moraines has created placer deposits of [[Gold]] in southernmost Chile. The term was introduced into geology by Horace Bénédict de Saussure in 1779.

American actor, producer and narrator. Freeman rose to fame in the 1970s on the children's television series *The Electric Company*. He won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Supporting Actor for playing a former boxer in [[Clint Eastwood]]'s *Million Dollar Baby* (2004), and was nominated for *Driving Miss Daisy* and [[The Shawshank Redemption]]. He portrayed Lucius Fox in the *Dark Knight* films of [[Christopher Nolan]]. Known for his voice, he narrated documentaries including *March of the Penguins* (2005). In 1996 he founded the production company Revelations Entertainment with Lori McCreary; its productions include the [[CBS]] political drama *Madam Secretary*.

Powerful and ambiguous enchantress from the legend of [[King Arthur]]. Morgan may be a fairy or a human, beneficial or harmful, and a sister or unrelated to Arthur. Geoffrey of Monmouth's *Vita Merlini* (c. 1150), the earliest account, presents her as a healer and leader of nine sisters on the Isle of Apples, Avalon. In 13th-century prose cycles she is usually Arthur's half-sister and a villain who schemes against Guinevere and the court. In some later versions she is Arthur's greatest enemy, but she eventually reconciles with him and carries him to Avalon. Her modern character is often conflated with her sister, the Queen of [[Orkney]], mother of Mordred.

Theology and religious tradition of the Latter Day Saint movement, a Restorationist Christian movement started by [[Joseph Smith]] in western New York in the 1820s and 1830s. Mormon theology combines mainstream Christian belief with modifications stemming from revelations to Smith and other leaders. It uses the [[Bible]] along with the Book of Mormon, published in 1830, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price. Doctrines include eternal marriage, baptism for the dead and, formerly, plural marriage. The Utah-based [[The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints|LDS Church]] banned [[Polygamy]] in 1890 and does not affirm Trinitarianism, which groups such as the Community of Christ do. Since 2018 the LDS Church has pushed to distance itself from the label.

Smallest meaningful constituent of a linguistic expression, especially within a word. A free morpheme can stand alone as a word, such as *town*, while a bound morpheme appears only within words, such as the *-s* in *cats*. Bound morphemes include affixes, such as prefixes and suffixes, and roots that cannot stand alone, such as the [[Latin]] *reg-* in *regis*. Derivational morphemes change meaning or part of speech, as the suffix *-ness* does in turning *happy* into *happiness*. Inflectional morphemes add grammatical information without changing word class, and English has eight inflections. Allomorphs are variants of one morpheme, such as the three pronunciations of the English plural marker. The study of morphemes is [[Morphology (linguistics)|morphology]].

Opiate analgesic found naturally in [[Opium]], a resin from the latex of opium poppies (*[[Papaver somniferum]]*). It is used mainly for severe acute and chronic [[Pain]], including pain from myocardial infarction, kidney stones and labor. It acts directly on the central nervous system, and dependence, tolerance and withdrawal may develop with repeated use. Common side effects include drowsiness, nausea and constipation; serious ones include decreased respiratory effort and low blood pressure. German pharmacist Friedrich Sertürner first isolated it in 1804, and Merck began marketing it in 1827. The name honors Morpheus, the god of dreams. Approximately 523 tons were produced in 2013, and about 70% was used to make other [[Opioid|opioids]] such as [[Heroin]]. It is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines.

Branch of [[Linguistics]] that studies how words are formed and how they relate to one another. Morphology analyzes words in terms of [[Morpheme|morphemes]], the smallest units with independent meaning or grammatical function. A root such as *catch* can be a word by itself, while an affix such as *-ing* appears only in larger words. The field also examines how words behave as parts of speech and how they are inflected for number, tense and aspect. Morphology operates at a larger scale than [[Phonology]] and a smaller scale than [[Syntax]]. Ancient Indian analysis dates to [[Pāṇini]], who formulated 3,959 rules of [[Sanskrit]] morphology. The term was introduced into linguistics by August Schleicher in 1859.

Telecommunications method that encodes text as standardized sequences of two signal durations, called dots and dashes or dits and dahs. A dah lasts three times as long as a dit, and the letters of a word are separated by a space of three dits. The ITU International Morse code covers the 26 [[Latin alphabet|Latin letters]], the numerals 0 to 9, some punctuation and procedural signals, with no distinction between upper and lower case. [[Samuel Morse]] devised a preliminary code, but the alphabet was developed by Alfred Vail, whose version was used for commercial [[Telegraphy]] in North America, while Friedrich Gerke's revision became the European standard. Morse code is usually sent by on-off keying of an electric current, [[Radio]] waves, light or sound. It remains in use for distress signals such as SOS and in [[Amateur radio]].

American media franchise centered on a series of fighting [[Video game|video games]], originally developed by Midway Games in 1992. The original [[Arcade game|arcade game]] spawned action-adventure games, a comic book series, a card game, film series and an animated TV series. The franchise is the best-selling fighting game series, with over 100 million copies sold. It is known for graphic violence, especially its fatalities, which kill defeated opponents instead of knocking them out. Controversy over this violence helped lead to the creation of the Entertainment Software Rating Board rating system. After Midway's bankruptcy, the development team was acquired by Warner Bros. Entertainment and re-established as NetherRealm Studios.

Short-barreled [[Artillery]] piece that fires explosive shells in high arcing trajectories. A modern mortar is usually a lightweight, man-portable, muzzle-loaded tube fixed to a base plate and bipod, used for indirect close fire support. Historically, mortars were heavy siege artillery. The earliest reported use was in a 1413 naval battle in Korea, where gunsmiths used gourd-shaped wan'gu mortars. In 1701 Baron Menno van Coehoorn invented a transportable mortar that fired a shell fused by hot gases on firing, which led to the bomb vessel. Mortars were heavily used in the [[American Civil War]], and at the 1863 Siege of Vicksburg [[Ulysses S. Grant|Ulysses S. Grant]] reported making them from logs. Short-range trench mortars were fired from frontline trenches in [[World War I]].

Loan secured on real property, which the lender can take through foreclosure to repay the debt if the borrower defaults. Mortgages are used by home buyers and by owners raising funds for any purpose. The lender is usually a [[Bank]], credit union or building society, and its rights over the property take priority over the borrower's other creditors. In the United States, mortgages typically amortize over 30 years. Many countries fund home purchases this way. Mortgages may be funded through bank deposits or through securitization, which converts pools of mortgages into [[Bond (finance)|bonds]] sold to investors. The word derives from a Law French term meaning *death pledge*, as the pledge ends when the obligation is fulfilled or the property is taken.

Genus of about 17 species of deciduous [[Tree|trees]], known as mulberries, in the family [[Moraceae]]. The genus is native to warm-temperate and tropical regions of Asia, eastern and southern North America and northwestern South America. Its three most common forms are named white, red and black for the colour of their dormant buds: *Morus alba*, *M. rubra* and *M. nigra*. *Morus alba* is native to China, is widely cultivated and is the species most preferred by the silkworm [[Bombyx mori]], so the genus is important in sericulture. It is regarded as invasive in Brazil, the United States and some Australian states. Mulberries are not closely related to raspberries or blackberries, which belong to the family Rosaceae. Taxonomy is complex and disputed, and hybridization between species is widespread.

Pattern or image made of small pieces of colored stone, glass or ceramic, held in place by mortar or plaster and covering a surface. Mosaics are mostly used as floor and wall decoration. They date to Mesopotamia in the 3rd millennium BC, and pebble mosaics appeared at Tiryns in Mycenaean Greece. Figural mosaics became widespread in [[Ancient Greece|Greece]] and [[Ancient Rome|Rome]], where large floor mosaics enriched villas and dwellings. Early Christian basilicas from the 4th century were decorated with wall and ceiling mosaics, and the art flourished in the [[Byzantine Empire]] from the 6th to the 15th centuries. Early Islamic religious buildings used mostly non-figurative mosaics, including at the Dome of the Rock in [[Jerusalem]]. Modern mosaics may use shells, beads, coins and other found materials.

Extinct genus of large marine [[Lizard|lizards]] from the Late Cretaceous. Its first fossils were skulls found in a [[Chalk]] quarry near Maastricht and were initially thought to be crocodiles or whales. In 1808 [[Georges Cuvier]] concluded that it was a giant marine lizard, an idea that helped support the developing concept of [[Extinction]]. The largest species, *M. hoffmanni*, may reach 12 meters. It had paddle-like limbs, a powerful tail fluke and dozens of large teeth. Its diet probably included fish, sharks, [[Cephalopod|cephalopods]], birds and other marine reptiles. Its exact relationship to modern lizards and snakes remains debated.

Synthetic [[Chemical element|chemical element]] with symbol Mc and atomic number 115. It was first synthesized in 2003 by a joint team of Russian and American scientists at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia. It was officially named in 2016 after the Moscow Oblast, where the institute is situated. All known isotopes are extremely radioactive. In the [[Periodic table]] it is the heaviest member of group 15. It is calculated to have properties similar to [[Bismuth]] and [[Thallium]], and experiments on single atoms have confirmed that it is less reactive than bismuth.

Public research university in Moscow, Russia, officially M. V. Lomonosov Moscow State University. The university was established in 1755, after Ivan Shuvalov and [[Mikhail Lomonosov]] promoted the idea and Empress Elizabeth decreed its establishment. It includes 15 research institutes, 43 faculties, more than 300 departments and six branches. Alumni include past leaders of the [[Soviet Union]] and other governments. In the Imperial era the university was the scene of student unrest, and in 1911 130 scientists and professors resigned in protest. Since 1992 it has been funded directly from the state budget. As of 2019, 13 Nobel laureates, 6 [[Fields Medal|Fields Medal]] winners and 1 Turing Award winner were affiliated with it.

Place of worship for Muslims, also called a masjid. The term usually refers to a covered building but can be any place where [[Islam|Islamic]] prayers are performed, such as an outdoor courtyard. Mosques typically have a mihrab, a niche in the wall marking the direction of [[Mecca]], and a facility for ritual cleansing. The pulpit, or minbar, is used for Friday sermons. Mosques also host funerals, marriages and religious instruction, and have historically served as community centers and courts of law. The three most important are al-Masjid al-Haram in Mecca, the Prophet's Mosque in [[Medina]], and al-Aqsa Mosque in [[Jerusalem]]. After the early Muslim conquests, many synagogues, churches and temples were converted into mosques.

Family of small [[Fly|flies]], the Culicidae, consisting of about 3,600 species. Mosquitoes have one pair of wings and a long proboscis adapted for piercing and sucking. All mosquitoes drink nectar, and females of many species also drink blood, which some species need before they can lay eggs. Their life cycle has four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult, with the first three largely aquatic. Some mosquitoes carry protozoan parasites or viruses from one host to another, including the vectors of [[Malaria]], filariasis, [[Yellow fever]] and [[Dengue fever]]. The group diversified during the [[Cretaceous]] period. Larvae feed on algae and organic material and are an important food source for many freshwater animals.

Small, typically non-vascular flowerless plant in the division Bryophyta. Mosses form dense green clumps or mats, often in damp or shady places, with leaves usually only one cell thick. They do not have seeds and reproduce with [[Spore|spores]] released from a [[Sporophyte]] capsule. Unlike vascular plants, the haploid [[Gametophyte]] generation is dominant in the life cycle. Mosses absorb water and nutrients mainly through their leaves. Most peat is made of mosses, mostly the genus [[Sphagnum]], and mosses are also used in gardens and the florist trade. They help stop [[Erosion|erosion]], improve microclimate and absorb carbon, with mosses estimated to absorb 6.4 billion tons of carbon annually. The tallest moss, *Dawsonia superba*, can grow to 60 centimeters.
